## Key interpretive findings

### 1. Detection barely separates real features from random directions — discrimination is the informative battery

Random-init detection reads 0.672 [0.640, 0.702] vs real 0.704 [0.688, 0.718]: a 0.032 gap with nearly touching CIs, while shuffled-label sits at 0.514. Reading: given ANY consistent linear direction (trained or random), the describer can summarize what its top-activating windows share, and that summary detects held-out activating windows at ~0.67–0.70. Detection accuracy is therefore mostly a property of the describe-then-judge instrument, not of SAE feature quality — consistent with the "random directions read as describable" side of the 2410.13928-vs-2501.17727 contradiction the plan flagged (control REPORTED, not gated, exactly for this reason). Discrimination, which requires the description to individuate the feature among its neighbours, is where the instrument actually resolves quality — and it fails at 0.322. Per-feature distributions (supporting figure 1): 328/650 features score exactly 0 on discrimination; the real and random-init detection histograms substantially overlap.

### 2. The discrimination failure is NOT explained by decoder-space near-duplicate features

Alternative explanations considered for the decisive fail:

- **(a) SAE near-duplicates (dictionary property):** rejected for decoder cosine. Top-neighbour decoder cosine in the val sample is LOW (median 0.33, p90 0.48; only 2.7% of all 16,384 features have a top neighbour above 0.6), and per-feature discrimination does not fall with neighbour cosine — Spearman ρ = +0.05 (p = 0.19, n=650); the highest-cosine bins score slightly BETTER (0.38 at cos ≥ 0.45 vs 0.30 at cos < 0.3). Residual caveat: neighbours could still be near-duplicates in ACTIVATION space (co-firing) without decoder-cosine similarity; untested here.
- **(b) Descriptions too generic (description property):** supported. 76.6% of features are labeled `syntax` (content_type), and the spot-check descriptions are dominated by broad function-word/punctuation summaries — a description like "list-separating punctuation across languages" detects activating windows fine but cannot pick the feature's own window out of 3 neighbours whose windows contain similar frequent-token text. Genericity is rewarded by detection and punished only by discrimination, which is exactly the observed pattern. `describe_confidence` correlates with detection (Spearman ρ = 0.42, p ≈ 2e-22, n=480), so the describer partially knows when it has a grounded description.
- **(c) Battery too hard (instrument property):** partially plausible — the 4-way choice uses 32-token windows from one shared corpus, and item-level chance-adjusted headroom is small (1–3 items/feature survived judging; scores quantized to {0, ⅓, ½, ⅔, 1}) — but shuffled controls landing at floor and real landing above chance show the battery is functioning; "too hard" cannot explain the 0.18 shortfall to the bar by itself.

Net: the leading explanation is (b), with (a)-in-activation-space unexcluded. Either way the operational conclusion is the same — the descriptions individuate features too weakly to carry per-feature headlines.

### 3. Validation batteries carry heavy judge-side item censoring (content drops 46–72% per arm) — verdict robust, point estimates soft

The scorecard drop counters: detection 1,270 / fuzzing 1,252 / discrimination 1,036 content drops, 0 transport — against 2,294 / 1,900 / 2,256 launched items. Per-arm item drop rates (error/missing/malformed-answers predicate over `val_results_*.json`): detection real 55.3% (832/1,504), shuffled 50.3% (199/396), random-init 53.3% (210/394) — roughly arm-symmetric; fuzzing real 63.7% (958/1,504) vs shuffled 72.2% (286/396) — an 8.5 pp ASYMMETRY with the shuffled arm dropping MORE, so the 0.502 shuffled-fuzzing control value is a censored-subset mean; discrimination is a SINGLE-arm battery (1,036/2,256 = 45.9% dropped), so arm symmetry cannot support robustness there at all. Feature-level attrition follows: 272/752 real features lost entirely from detection, 319/752 from fuzzing, 102/752 from discrimination. The dropped returns are overwhelmingly `parse_error` dicts (e.g. detection: 1,241 errors, all `reasoning: parse_error`, `transport: false`), and the few surviving malformed rows show long free-form rationales with no parseable answer block. With `VAL_MAX_TOKENS = 400` on a reason-then-answer rubric spanning 6 windows per item, this is the llm-judging rule-23 truncation signature (the #1090 shape) — leading hypothesis, unverified here (stop_reason not persisted in the parsed dicts).

(iii) A re-judge of the dropped items at a larger response budget against a fresh cache is the standard rule-23 remedy and is the top follow-up below. === 2. THE PARSE MECHANISM, VERIFIED IN SOURCE ===
`eval/utils.py::parse_judge_json` tries `json.loads(text)`, then falls back to
`start = text.index("{")` + `raw_decode(text, start)` — it anchors on the FIRST
brace in the response. Its docstring already claims tolerance of "markdown
fences, preamble", so this is a stated-intent-vs-behaviour gap, not a missing
feature.

The consequence explains the rates precisely: a CLEANLY fenced response parses
fine, because the first `{` is the real object (my axes probe saw 35/60 fenced
and 60/60 parse). Failures are the narrower subset where a brace appears BEFORE
the object — a preamble or reasoning prose containing `{`, which sends
`raw_decode` at the wrong offset. That is why fencing at ~58% yields only ~2%
failures, and why stripping to the fenced block recovers 29/40: the strip skips
the offending preamble.

| 0.10 | 22.56 | 0.97 |
